clinicalPearls: Presents with acute, often itchy or burning, oedematous erythematous plaques that closely resemble bacterial cellulitis but fail to respond to antibiotics and lack fever
Lesions may evolve over days into slate-grey or greenish infiltrated plaques as they resolve, and the eruption tends to recur
It is a reactive hypersensitivity process rather than an infection, often triggered by insect bites, drugs, infections or, occasionally, underlying haematological disease
Peripheral blood eosinophilia is common but not invariable
The histological hallmark is dermal eosinophilic infiltration with 'flame figures', formed by eosinophil granule proteins coating collagen bundles
Diagnosis rests on recognising the mismatch between a cellulitis-like appearance and the biopsy findings
Treatment is with systemic corticosteroids for troublesome disease and identification of any trigger; many cases eventually remit
reference.pathophysiology: Wells syndrome is thought to represent a hypersensitivity reaction with abnormal eosinophil recruitment and activation in the skin, often in response to an identifiable stimulus such as an arthropod bite, drug, infection or underlying disorder. Activated eosinophils infiltrate the dermis and degranulate, depositing major basic protein and other granule proteins onto collagen fibres to create the characteristic flame figures, surrounded by histiocytes and giant cells in later stages. This eosinophil-driven tissue reaction produces the oedematous, cellulitis-like plaques and their tendency to recur.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy demonstrating tissue eosinophilia and flame figures
Full blood count for peripheral eosinophilia
Investigation for triggers (recent bites, drugs, infections)
Stool examination for parasites where relevant
Evaluation for underlying haematological or myeloproliferative disease in persistent cases
Inflammatory markers to help distinguish from infective cellulitis
redFlags: Marked or persistent eosinophilia suggesting hypereosinophilic syndrome with organ involvement
Failure to respond, prompting reassessment for underlying malignancy or myeloproliferative disease
Genuine secondary bacterial infection of oedematous skin
Extensive or blistering lesions with systemic upset
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but characteristically relapsing, with individual episodes resolving over weeks, sometimes leaving transient discoloration; most patients eventually enter remission, though recurrent flares can be troublesome and steroid-dependent.
pitfalls: Repeatedly treating it as bacterial cellulitis with escalating antibiotics
Not biopsying antibiotic-unresponsive 'cellulitis' to reveal the eosinophilic pattern
Assuming flame figures are specific, when they occur in other eosinophil-rich dermatoses
Overlooking an underlying haematological disorder in persistent or severe cases
management: Identify and remove precipitating triggers such as arthropod bites, culprit drugs and infections
Topical or tapering systemic corticosteroids as the mainstay for symptomatic oedematous plaques
Oral antihistamines for pruritus and symptomatic relief
Steroid-sparing agents such as dapsone or ciclosporin, or anti-IL-5 biologics, for relapsing or steroid-dependent disease
Confirm the diagnosis on biopsy and avoid unnecessary prolonged antibiotics given the mimicry of bacterial cellulitis
Investigate for and manage underlying haematological or myeloproliferative disease in persistent cases
Dermatology referral for recurrent or refractory disease
